title: From Conception to Birth

html:
By birth, the brain’s optimization architecture is already scaffolded: the learning loops are anatomically in place and their teacher channels wired, even if connectivity (including long- and short-range connectivity) is only coarsely specified (all major white matter tracts are, however, identifiable by the end of normal gestation 1). Cortico-cerebellar microcomplexes are formed (mossy fibers from pontine relays and climbing fibers from inferior olive converge on Purkinje dendrites and deep nuclei), establishing a supervised-calibration pathway with fractured somatotopy and strong temporal precision. Basal ganglia actor-critic loops are closed: cortex projects to a compartmentalized striatum (D1/D2, patch/matrix), midbrain dopamine reaches striatum and pallidum, and thalamo-cortical return paths exist, yielding an RL substrate with innate action-selection competition and a burst/pause teaching signal. Cortico-thalamo-cortical hierarchies are laminated and topographic-retino-/tono-/somatotopy are present, layer-4 relay and feedback layers are differentiated, and higher-order thalamus (pulvinar/MD) provides the long-range gating needed for predictive-coding-like inference. The hippocampal-entorhinal trisynaptic loop is assembled, and the major long-range conduits (corticospinal tract, corpus callosum, fornix, cingulum) are laid down but lightly myelinated, imposing bandwidth and latency constraints that may act as inductive biases on what can be learned first. Across the brainstem and forebrain, neuromodulatory tone (ACh, NE, DA, 5-HT) is established and the chloride-transport "GABA switch" around birth re-times excitability, effectively opening and closing gates on plasticity. These architectural priors–topography, center-surround inhibition, temporal precision in the olive, winner-take-most competition in BG, hierarchical feedforward/feedback loops in cortex–mean the newborn does not learn with a blank slate; it starts with biased, coarsely wired optimizers that need calibration (a lot of it).

Taking it a step further, by late gestation, the brain is not merely a bag of partially-wired modules; it already exhibits a system-level communication scaffold. Macroscale connectivity is organized according to a cost-value compromise: strongly clustered, modular local circuits coupled by a sparse set of long-range routes that disproportionately link hub regions (a core-periphery / rich-club-like backbone; see "The Semantic Memory System") 2, 3, 4. Importantly, this "global graph" is not purely structural: in utero resting-state dynamics already reveal recognizable large-scale functional networks–sensorimotor/visual/thalamic systems appear first and are detectable by mid-gestation, while higher-order association networks (default-mode/frontoparietal/salience-like components) emerge later in the third trimester and remain spatially fragmented and weakly segregated compared to postnatal patterns 5, 6, 7, 8. So the right way to phrase the "degree" of prenatally identifiable network structure is: the backbone and community structure are already present as a coarse, biased scaffold, with rapidly increasing long-range and interhemispheric coupling late in gestation, but the adult-like sharpness of network boundaries and the reliable, high-bandwidth timing of long-range coordination (and thus fully fledged "global workspace-like" broadcasting) remain immature until postnatal myelination, synaptic/inhibitory stabilization, and continued circuit refinement. A 2025 study examines early human thalamic development (Figure) 81. The study summarizes developmental molecular gradients (Figure).

Pillars of Gestational Learning

Molecular patterning and cell migration can be seen as the "zeroth pillar" of gestational learning. Long before sensory-driven learning, the cortex is "pretrained" by gradients and lineage programs that set where computations will live and how information will flow. Competing-but-compatible frames–protomap (intrinsic areal identity from morphogen gradients) and protocortex (extrinsic refinement via extrinsic (especially thalamic) input)–together explain why early cortex is neither blank nor fully specified: it is biased, scaffolded, and then data-aligned 9, 10. Meanwhile, inside-out lamination via radial glial cells and long-range tangential migration (parallel to the brain’s surface) of interneurons from ganglionic eminences supply the canonical cortical microcircuit parts list (projection neurons in layers, inhibitory classes arriving on schedule), with transient populations such as Cajal-Retzius cells (which produce reelin, an extracellular matrix protein) shaping final layer placement 11, 12, 13. This is "initializing" the brain in the literal sense: a structured hypothesis class is built before experience tunes parameters. A 2025 atlas maps gene expression in human fetal cortex (Figure) 79. The atlas examines formation of cortical layers (Figure).

The first pillar of gestational learning is patterned spontaneous activity: before the senses open to the world, peripheral organs and central circuits generate structured "proto-data" that calibrate maps and controllers. In vision, retinal waves–coherent, spatially local bursts that propagate across the immature retina–drive correlated activity through the optic nerve into downstream relays, where they refine (rather than solely create) topographic organization laid down by molecular guidance cues, sharpening retinotopy in targets such as the lateral geniculate nucleus and superior colliculus and promoting eye-specific segregation and competitive alignment 14, 15, 16. This is not noise; it is a low-dimensional curriculum: the dominant prenatal patterns are constrained (e.g., wavefronts and bursts), meaning that despite rich single-neuron variability, population activity often lies on a small set of recurring spatiotemporal modes (location/phase, direction, speed, amplitude). These modes implicitly implement priors that later perception will rely on: topographic continuity (nearby sensors co-activate), temporal coherence (states evolve smoothly via propagating fronts), and local correlation structure (activity is clustered rather than globally synchronous) 17, 18, 19. Importantly, this does not mean the fetus "learns to detect edges" in the adult sense; rather, it initializes the wiring geometry and gain structure that make oriented, localized receptive fields an easy downstream solution once real images arrive. In vision specifically, wave statistics can bias circuits toward the kinds of anisotropic correlations that later support orientation-/direction-selective organization and map alignment 20, 19. Similar low-dimensional spontaneous regimes exist cortically (spindle bursts/early network oscillations, delta brushes) and somatosensorily, where thalamus-subplate-cortex loops rehearse the dialogue they will later run online 21, 22, 23, 24. One study connects the direction of retinal waves to the orientation map in the mouse superior colliculus (Figure).

Audition shows the same logic. Long before airborne sound is reliably transduced, inner hair cells and supporting epithelial networks in the cochlea fire organized bursts that sweep tonotopic space 25, 26, 27. At the population level this again resembles a low-dimensional generator (a burst packet whose latent variables include position along the tonotopic axis, spatial spread to neighboring channels, and inter-burst timing), which is exactly what map-refinement plasticity needs before high-dimensional natural sound statistics dominate 25, 27. These events walk the auditory pathway through its future feature basis (frequency channels and their co-activation patterns) so that, when acoustic input actually arrives near 25-27 gestational weeks for low frequencies and by  29-31 weeks for higher frequencies, the system is already partially tuned 28, 29. This staged opening means that much of "auditory pretraining" is self-generated, then smoothly handed off to real sound in late gestation. That handoff produces measurable fetal/neonatal plasticity to structured stimulation (e.g., repeated melodies or speech-like patterns), and the trace persists postnatally 30, 31, 32, 33.

The second pillar is the subplate, a transient but highly active cortical compartment that acts as a timed interface between incoming thalamic drive and an immature cortical plate. Thalamic axons reach the appropriate cortical territory before layer-4 targets are ready; they form provisional synapses and "wait" within the subplate, then invade the cortical plate once targets mature–effectively routing and pacing early sensory drive into nascent circuits 34, 35, 36. Subplate neurons are among the earliest-born cortical neurons and form one of the first functional cortical networks: they receive thalamic input (and are positioned to integrate diffuse neuromodulatory signals) and project into the developing cortical plate, providing a temporary excitatory/organizational scaffold that can amplify weak thalamic signals, synchronize local activity, and bias where thalamic branches stabilize during the waiting-to-invasion transition 37. During late fetal and early neonatal periods, subplate-coupled circuitry participates in prominent spindle-burst and related early oscillations; these patterned events are thought to supply precisely the kind of structured, repeatable training signal" needed for activity-dependent refinement–guiding axonal branching, target selection, map sharpening, and synaptic stabilization along thalamocortical pathways when peripheral inputs are sparse and cortical microcircuits are still being assembled 38, 39. Disruption of subplate development (including injury affecting subplate/white matter compartments) is associated with durable neurocognitive deficits, consistent with the idea that this transient relay exerts lasting control over when and where early instructive signals land–and therefore over the initial conditions from which mature cortical architecture self-organizes 40, 41, 42. A study maps cell types in human fetal cortex (Figure) 80. The study resolves the fetal subplate (Figure). The authors examine subplate-neuron origins (Figure).

A third pillar is fetal motor babbling and reafference. Spontaneous self-generated movements begin in the first trimester (with an expanding repertoire from whole-body to limb-specific actions), ensuring that even before rich exteroceptive input is available, the fetus is bathed in structured proprioceptive, vestibular, and tactile consequences of its own actions–including "double touch" during self-contact (touching hand + touched face) that naturally labels body boundaries and seeds somatotopic organization 43, 44, 45. In late gestation, spontaneous twitches and multi-joint movements are expressed prominently during REM-like (active) sleep, indexed in humans by characteristic eye-movement bouts and embedded within organized ultradian sleep cycling (with active/REM-like sleep comprising a large fraction of fetal state time) 21, 46, 47, 48. Each twitch is a labeled event: a motor event paired with precisely timed reafferent feedback that calibrates developing spinal/brainstem controllers, builds sensorimotor contingencies, and drives activity-dependent refinement of sensorimotor circuits–including nascent cerebellar computations consistent with forward-model learning 49, 50. Importantly, reafferent processing is state dependent: expected reafference is gated during wake-related self-generated movements, but this gating is reduced/absent during active-sleep twitches, allowing twitches–despite being self-generated–to robustly propagate error-like sensory signals upstream and support credit assignment 51, 50, 49. Because active sleep occupies such a high fraction of time in late gestation and the early neonatal period, gestation provides a massive, low-cost reservoir of self-supervised (motor, sensory) tuples that initialize postnatal goal-directed control long before the infant explicitly "intends" an action 21, 46.

The fourth pillar is a sequential, low-to-high dimensional sensory curriculum whose "stage 0" is internally generated activity. Early gestation is dominated by low-bandwidth, highly redundant streams (visceroceptive rhythms, full-field tactile pressure, vestibular sway) plus patterned spontaneous bursts/waves that act as synthetic "proto-inputs"; only later do higher-entropy, high-dimensional channels (external acoustics, then vision) ramp up and reshape representations 52, 21, 28, 53. This ordering parcels experience from low- to high-dimensional streams: stable, slowly varying signals (cardiac and respiratory rhythms, visceroceptive cycles, steady contact) can pretrain temporal integrators and priors, while higher-bandwidth channels ramp later to enrich the representational manifold. Only late in gestation do external airborne acoustics become behaviorally salient 28, 54 (after weeks of primarily low-pass, internally generated sound), and vision may largely be deferred until after birth 53, 55, 56. The result is a curriculum that eases optimization–preventing early representational collapse, minimizing interference, and aligning emerging controllers with reliable state estimation before the sensory firehose opens. A helpful intuition is manifold expansion: early learning happens on a small, stable set of latent modes (waves/bursts/rhythms), and later sensory experience increases dimensionality and specificity without forcing the optimizer to search the full space from scratch 19, 18.

This curriculum installs statistical structure that the postnatal learner will exploit. Maternal speech prosody and repeated melodies leave durable neural traces; newborns show ERP signatures of having learned specific auditory patterns in utero and even display production biases that mirror native-language intonation in their cries 31, 32, 30. Chemosensory exposure provides another early "real-world" channel: flavors and odors from the maternal diet diffuse into the amniotic fluid, biasing early preferences and anchoring hedonic baselines (i.e value priors tuned to local ecology) 57, 58. A 2025 study tests responses to rhythm in preterm infants (Figure) 82. The preterm-infant study maps auditory responses (Figure).

The fifth pillar is neuromodulatory scheduling and hormonal gating. In early gestation, the placenta converts maternal tryptophan into serotonin and delivers it to the fetal forebrain before raphe inputs arrive, where 5-HT functions as a developmental signal that biases axon growth and sensory map formation (notably via 5-HT1B/1D pathways); this makes the placental-maternal state a plausible lever on the neurochemical context the newborn inherits 59, 60. Around birth, inhibitory tone undergoes the canonical NKCC1->KCC2 chloride-transport switch, shifting GABAA action from predominantly depolarizing to hyperpolarizing and retiming network dynamics as giant depolarizing potentials and other synchronous neonatal patterns give way to sparser, adult-like regimes 61, 62, 63. In vivo and review work converge that this maturation of inhibition is a prerequisite for opening and closing classic critical-period windows-i.e., it sets when and where Hebbian changes can be expressed-which justifies reading "plasticity’s sign, gain, and spatial reach" as developmentally scheduled control knobs 64, 65. Several of these knobs are also coupled to maternal-placental inputs: the placental serotonin pathway is sensitive to maternal physiology and inflammation, and the 11β-HSD2 barrier in placenta buffers fetal exposure to glucocorticoids that modulate excitability and plasticity thresholds, providing concrete mechanisms by which extrinsic state can tune the initial learning conditions 66, 67, 68, 69.

Sleep is the sixth pillar: by late gestation it occupies the vast majority of time, dominated by active (REM-like) sleep 70, 71. This state is saturated with developmental burst patterns, which may coordinate thalamocortical and hippocampo-cortical communication while gating plasticity 72, 73. During active sleep, the aforementioned spontaneous twitches and organ-driven rhythms send precisely timed reafferent volleys through spinal cord, brainstem, thalamus, cerebellum, and sensorimotor cortex, supplying labeled motor-sensory tuples that pretrain forward models and calibrate gains well before intentional action. Across these long offline windows, sleep-dependent mechanisms consolidate useful assemblies (those with high inter-neuronal resonance) and prune maladaptive ones 21, 74, 75, 76, so the system emerges with cleaner, more stable controllers.

It is worth emphasizing that gestation doesn’t only add synapses; it also sculpts circuits by deleting cells/branches that fail to integrate. Programmed cell death is widespread in developing brain and participates in morphogenesis, controlling population sizes and removing transient scaffolds 77, 78. Interpreted computationally, apoptosis + synapse elimination behave like an L0/L1-style constraint on gestational circuit complexity: overspecify early, then compress toward efficient solutions consistent with spontaneous and peripheral-driven activity statistics (a process that plays out across the lifespan, but is perhaps most present during gestation). On this view, early low-dimensional motifs act like a stabilizing training signal: circuits that resonate with (and can reliably predict / reproduce) the dominant prenatal modes are preferentially stabilized, while branches that fail to participate in coherent assemblies are more likely to be eliminated–compression not just of parameters, but of dynamics 21, 77.

Conclusion

In sum, the prenatal brain is not passively awaiting experience but actively constructing the preconditions for learning. Molecular gradients and migratory programs establish a coarse computational blueprint; patterned spontaneous activity (retinal waves, cochlear bursts, spindle-burst oscillations) provides a low-dimensional synthetic curriculum that sharpens maps and initializes gain structures before the corresponding sensory channels open. The subplate orchestrates when and where thalamic signals first engage cortex, while fetal motor babbling and state-gated reafference supply labeled sensorimotor tuples that pretrain forward models. Layered atop this is a naturalistic curriculum in which low-bandwidth, highly redundant streams (visceroceptive rhythms, vestibular sway, filtered maternal speech) give way to progressively higher-dimensional input, easing optimization by expanding the representational manifold incrementally rather than all at once. Neuromodulatory and hormonal schedules (placental serotonin, the peri-birth GABA polarity switch, glucocorticoid gating) set the when and where of plasticity, while prolonged active sleep provides the offline state in which twitches, bursts, and consolidation mechanisms refine and compress emerging circuits. By birth, therefore, the newborn inherits not a blank slate but a richly biased, coarsely wired optimization engine: learning loops are closed, teaching signals are routed, and statistical priors (topographic continuity, temporal coherence, local correlation structure, and even culture-specific auditory templates) are already written into the hardware, ready to be calibrated by the postnatal world.
